problem.text: Many states use a sequence of three letters followed by a sequence of three digits as their standard license-plate pattern. Given that each three-letter three-digit arrangement is equally likely, the probability that such a license plate will contain at least one palindrome (a three-letter arrangement or a three-digit arrangement that reads the same left-to-right as it does right-to-left) is $\frac{m}{n}$, where $m$ and $n$ are relatively prime positive integers. Find $m+n$.

steps.title: Where to start: handle the digits and the letters separately
steps.body: The plate has two independent parts, the three digits and the three letters. "At least one palindrome" means the digit part is a palindrome, or the letter part is, or both. So first find the chance for each part on its own.

your_turn.prompt: A three-digit string (leading zeros allowed) is a palindrome when it looks like $aba$. How many such strings are there, out of how many total?
your_turn.answer: $10^2 = 100$ palindromes out of $10^3 = 1000$ strings, since choosing $a$ and $b$ fixes the third digit.

steps.title: The two separate probabilities
steps.body:
The same idea works for letters with $26$ choices instead of $10$: the first letter fixes the last one.
$$P(\text{digits}) = \frac{10^2}{10^3} = \frac{1}{10}, \qquad P(\text{letters}) = \frac{26^2}{26^3} = \frac{1}{26}$$

your_turn.prompt: Why can't we just add $\frac{1}{10} + \frac{1}{26}$ to get the answer?
your_turn.answer: Plates where both parts are palindromes would be counted twice.

steps.title: Subtract the overlap
steps.body: By inclusion-exclusion, $P(\text{A or B}) = P(\text{A}) + P(\text{B}) - P(\text{both})$. The digits and letters are chosen independently, so the chance that both are palindromes is the product of the two chances. Careful: forgetting this subtraction is the most common mistake here.

your_turn.prompt: What is the probability that both parts are palindromes?

steps.title: Put it together
steps.body:
Use $260$ as a common denominator.
$$\frac{1}{10} + \frac{1}{26} - \frac{1}{260} = \frac{26 + 10 - 1}{260} = \frac{35}{260} = \frac{7}{52}$$
Since $7$ and $52$ share no factor, $m = 7$ and $n = 52$, so $m + n = 59$. The answer is **$59$**.
